Innominate substance (Schwalbe, 1881), the English form of substantia innominata (Schwalbe, 1881), was sanctioned by the Terminologia Anatomica (1998, p. 129). For the rostral end of the SI just over the OT see Heimer et al. (1987), who called it the ventral pallidum. For a seminal modern paper see Jones et al. (1976). This region was renamed the ventral pallidum (Heimer & Wilson, 1975), and then later divided by Heimer and colleagues into a rostral part now commonly referred to as the ventral pallidum and a caudal part referred to as part of the extended amygdala; see de Olmos & Heimer (1999), and a critique by Swanson (2003b). The innominate substance (Schwalbe, 1881) contains characteristic subpopulations of scattered, cortically projecting cholinergic and noncholinergic neurons (Rye et al., 1984) that in some animals (especially primates), but not in rats, form distinct cell clusters known as the basal nuclei of Meynert (see Gorry, 1963). These cholinergic neurons spread into the medial septal complex (Swanson et al. 1987), the magnocellular nucleus (Swanson, 2004), and perhaps to a very limited extent the lateral preoptic area (>1840). The term magnocellular basal “nucleus” was introduced (Saper, 1984) for referring to the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that project to the cerebral cortex (>1840). A developmental model for how the innominate substance (Schwalbe, 1881) comes to lie between three parts of the striatum (Swanson, 2000a), the accumbens nucleus (Ziehen, 1897-1901), striatal fundus (>1840), and olfactory tubercle (Calleja, 1893), has been presented elsewhere (Alvarez-Bolado et al., 1995).

This region comes as close to a basal nucleus of Meynert as anything in the rat; cholinergic neurons here innervate preferentially the olfactory bulb (Weitbrecht, 1751). It was originally named the magnocellular preoptic nucleus by Loo (1931) in opossum, but it seems doubtful if it is derived from third ventricular neuroepithelium during embryogenesis and thus “preoptic” was dropped from the name by Swanson (2004). Also see Swanson (1976a), Rye et al. (1984), and annotations for innominate substance (Schwalbe, 1881) and medial septal complex (Swanson et al., 1987).

There is no morphologically distinct boundary between this ventromedial region of the striatum (Swanson, 2000a) and the caudoputamen (Heimer & Wilson, 1975). Gurdjian (1928) first defined the accumbens nucleus (Ziehen, 1897-1901) in the rat as that part of the ventromedial striatum (Swanson, 2000a) lacking massive bundles of ascending and descending axons, which is still a useful working criterion. This term was introduced by Gurdjian (1928) to describe an ill-defined region that essentially all later workers have used somewhat differently, depending on how neighboring regions that are better differentiated have been described; we have followed in this tradition here.

We have followed McDonald's (1982) parceling into medial, lateral, and capsular parts, although it is clear that the nucleus is much more complex than this. McDonald's intermediate part was not recognized; it appears to fall within the lateral part as outlined here. The central amygdalar nucleus (Johnston, 1923) and medial amygdalar nucleus (Johnston, 1923) receive inputs from the cerebral cortex (>1840) and generate descending projections that are predominantly GABAergic, like the rest of the striatum (Swanson, 2000a). They also project to the bed nuclei of terminal stria (Gurdjian, 1925), regarded here as a component of the pallidum (Swanson, 2000a).

It is an olfactory cortical area, with a molecular layer and a pyramidal layer; see Haberly & Price (1978b), who noted that “the term nucleus is unfortunate since, in spite of the lack of cellular sublamination within these areas [retrobulbar], they are all clearly cortical in organization.” (p. 782). In the Discussion, they refer to “areas within the olfactory peduncle” (Haberly & Price, 1978b, p. 806). In this edition of Brain Maps, the name has been changed from anterior olfactory nucleus to anterior olfactory area to emphasize that it is a cerebral cortical area, not a subcortical nucleus. In addition, the five parts of Haberly & Price (1978b) that were listed in previous editions have been eliminated because they are based mostly on relative position, not cytoarchitectonically distinctive parts, except perhaps for a distinguishable external part. Thus, a principal part (AOApr) and an external part (AOAe) are delineated in the atlas. The detailed description and discussion of the rat AOA in De Olmos et al. (1978) is also quite useful. Neville & Haberly (2004, p. 416) referred to it as the anterior olfactory cortex.

There is little agreement in the literature about the parceling and nomenclature associated with the tenia tecta and indusium griseum. From examining sections in the three standard planes, it seems clear to us (Swanson, 1992a) that the indusium griseum (Valentin, 1841) in the rat continues uninterrupted around the genu of the corpus callosum to the septohippocampal nucleus (>1840) (Atlas Levels 11-13; also see Wyss & Sripanidkulchai, 1983). The part of the indusium griseum (Valentin, 1841) rostral and ventral to the genu was called the dorsal part of the tenia tecta by Haberly & Price (1978b). The ventral part of the tenia tecta of Haberly & Price (1978b) has a very different structure. They divided it into superior and inferior parts, referred to here as the dorsal and ventral parts of the tenia tecta proper, respectively (Swanson, 1992a). The tenia tecta (Swanson, 1992a) reminds one of differentiated parts of the adjacent anterior olfactory area (Herrick, 1910); see Davis et al. (1978). We recognize three layers in the TTv (as Haberly & Price, 1978b) and four layers in the TTd.

A clear difference between connections arising from the dorsal and ventral (also called septal and temporal) parts of field CA1 (Lorente de Nó, 1934) and the subiculum (>1840) goes back to early findings of Swanson & Cowan (1975, 1977). There are, however, no clear cytoarchitectonic borders, and for descriptive purposes may be divided by a line across the top of functional domain 2 in Figure 6 of Petrovich et al. (2001). In addition, it is often useful to indicate roughly dorsal, intermediate, and ventral (also called septal, occipital, and temporal) parts of field CA1 (Lorente de Nó, 1934) and the subiculum (>1840). This distinction goes back to the statement, “In a number of experiments the injections involved a region of the subiculum which, on topographic grounds, could not be described as either ‘dorsal’ or ‘ventral’ subiculum, but rather an intermediate zone…injections involving the dorsal subiculum always give rise to labeling over the dorsal part of the lateral septum, while intermediate and ventrally placed injections respectively labeled intermediate and ventral parts of the lateral septal nucleus.” (Swanson & Cowan, 1977, p. 68). For the name, and other clear dorsal-ventral distinctions of field CA1 (Lorente de Nó, 1934) and the subiculum (>1840) connections, see Canteras & Swanson (1992b), Risold & Swanson (1996, p. 1486 & Fig. 1); also see Cenquizca & Swanson (2006).

A simple distinction between medial and lateral parts of the entorhinal area (Brodmann, 1909) is followed; see Brodmann (1909), Hjorth-Simonsen & Jeune (1972), Swanson et al. (1978), Dolorfo & Amaral (1998b). Insausti et al. (1997) parceled their entorhinal area into 6 entorhinal fields. The entorhinal area medial part (>1840) contains their caudal (CE, field 1) and medial (ME, field 2) fields; the entorhinal area lateral part (>1840) contains their ventral intermediate (VIE, field 3), dorsal intermediate (DIE, field 4), and dorsal lateral (DLE, field 5) fields; and the postpiriform transition area (Canteras et al., 1992a) contains their amygdalo-entorhinal transition (AE, field 6) field. Postpiriform transition area (Canteras et al., 1992a) is not included here in the entorhinal area (Brodmann, 1909) because it does not project to the dentate gyrus (>1840) (see Petrovich, 1997; Dolorfo & Amaral, 1998a; Santiago & Shammah-Lagnado, 2005). Insausti et al. (1997) did not take into account the rostral extension of the entorhinal area medial part (>1840) called the ventral zone (ENTmv) in Swanson (1992a, 1998, 2004); see endnote for entorhinal area medial part (>1840). The general scheme followed here was also followed for practical purposes by Cappaert et al. (2015, p. 523).

Recent work has clarified the structural organization of the rat PAG, which is that part of what is traditionally called the central nervous system (Carus, 1814) central gray, within the midbrain (Baer, 1837). In this edition of the Atlas the basic parceling of the caudal three-quarters of the PAG, which originally followed Beitz (1985), has been revised to conform with the modifications introduced by Carrive et al. (1997) and refined by Comoli et al. (2003). Basically, the old dorsal division (PAGd) is renamed the dorsomedial column (PAGdm), the old dorsolateral division (PAGdl) is renamed the dorsolateral column, and the old ventrolateral column (PAGvl) is divided into a lateral column (PAGl), ventrolateral column (PAGvl), and ventromedial column (PAGvm). Paxinos & Watson (2007, Figures 80-106) was also useful in helping delineate these regions.

He divided the base of the dorsal horn (>1840) into medial and lateral basal nuclei—together called here the basal nucleus of dorsal horn general (1840), whereas his head and neck (dorsoventral center) of the dorsal horn (>1840) has come to be referred to as the nucleus proprius of spinal cord (>1840); the spinal reticular nucleus (>1840) is found lateral to the nucleus proprius of spinal cord (>1840) (see Rexed, 1952).
